statement: With art, story, meta-progression and juice stripped or toggled off, the 30-second core loop is still worth repeating.
The game contains a recurring choice whose best answer is neither obvious nor a blind guess.
That choice has stakes the target player cares about.
New patterns, tools or situations that demand new learning keep appearing until the end of the runtime.
The game exercises at least two distinct challenge types (cognitive, performative, emotional, decision-making).
Known strategies have counter-situations that punish rote repetition.
Skills learned early are prerequisites that unlock visibly new abilities or situations later.
Mastering one system makes sibling systems faster to learn.
After a failure, the player can say specifically what to do differently next time.
The game shows progress toward mastery clearly enough that improvement is felt without checking menus.
Post-play review of what happened (replays, run summaries) is available.
A spectator could tell a skilled player from a novice within a minute of watching.
The strongest feedback moments are attached to the actions that define skill in this game.
There is no single build, route or strategy that makes other options pointless.
Interesting decisions occur inside the core loop itself, not only in pause menus.
Making those decisions does not interrupt the flow of play.
Choices are trade-offs between goods, not puzzles with one right answer.
Players argue with each other about the best build, route or approach.
The consequences of earlier choices remain visible and traceable later.
The game gives enough foresight that an early, persistent choice cannot silently ruin a run.
The same obstacle can be beaten in more than one valid way.
Approaches the designers did not plan for still work.
The target player can set and pursue goals of their own inside the structure.
The player is never forced through long stretches of actions they did not choose.
The game's combination of goals, abilities and constraints feels like a specific way of being, recognisably different from other games.
Players describe the game by what it lets them do, not by its genre label.
Difficulty rises and falls in waves, guaranteeing both failures and successes on the way up.
The player can adjust effective difficulty from inside play (which fight, depth or route to take), not only from a settings menu.
Each challenge type the game uses is separately well-calibrated.
Opposition is neither trivially weak nor illegitimately advantaged.
Losing costs enough to matter but little enough that the player wants to retry immediately.
Failure never forces long mechanical replay of already-mastered content.
The player is never left with no way to finish (hopelessness).
Inputs map so reliably to outcomes that players blame themselves for failure — and are right to.
Random events resolve after the player's decision (affecting outcomes), not before it (invalidating plans).
Play is continuous: interruptions are player-initiated, not imposed.
The workload is high but within the player's perceptual and cognitive limits.
No task the game demands feels unimportant.
At the end of a loop there is always a concrete reason to play one more.
The game also offers natural stopping points where quitting feels clean.
The pull to continue coexists with high autonomy/competence satisfaction — it does not substitute for it.
Controls respond within the timing the game's actions demand (latency, buffering, cancel windows).
Every input is acknowledged instantly, at minimum with sound.
The state change caused by an action is readable before any embellishment plays.
Feedback strength scales with actual accomplishment, not with mere activity.
Layered juice stops short of obscuring what the player caused.
Objects move with believable weight and momentum.
The core movement or manipulation is pleasant with no goal at all.
Health, resources and threats are readable at a glance during action.
Detail is inspectable on demand without leaving play.
The game has music, not only sound effects.
Every effect is consistent with the world's physics and art style.
Interface chrome is themed to the world.
Sounds and voice lines are varied enough not to grate over a session.
At any moment the player can name a short-, a medium- and a long-term goal, all running simultaneously.
The outcome of the current arc stays genuinely uncertain until near its end.
The game uses at least two distinct uncertainty mechanisms (variable difficulty, multi-level goals, hidden information, randomness).
Progression regularly changes how the game is played, not only its numbers.
Intensity alternates deliberately — tension and release, novelty and consolidation.
The game engineers recurring moments of hard-won triumph that players remember.
New content or mechanics keep arriving through to the end of the runtime.
Discovery rewards are paced below the saturation point where opening one more feels like a chore.
Mechanics interact to produce outcomes nobody scripted.
Players trade 'did you know you can…' stories about the game.
The game plants questions the player wants answered.
The player believes those gaps are closable with effort.
Trying something weird produces an interesting result more often than a punishment.
Some worthwhile discoveries exist only for players who go looking.
The game lets the player be something they find appealing, and the mechanics deliver that fantasy.
The game evokes more than two distinct emotions in a normal playthrough.
At least one deliberately designed negative-valence peak (loss, dread, guilt) lands as memorable rather than merely unpleasant.
The skill depends on the fantasy and the fantasy depends on the skill (both directions).
A player's identity shows in their play — in builds, style or aesthetics.
Players report thinking about the game when not playing it.
Teaching is invisible inside play within the first minute.
Tutorial investment matches how much the mechanics genuinely need explaining.
The game never forces practice of an already-understood action.
Time in menus is a small fraction of session time.
A player can build a correct mental model of the rules from playing; surprises come from combination, not hidden information the game withheld unfairly.
Recovery from any error is quick — checkpoints and load times do not force replay.
Difficulty and control options broaden who can reach the game's designed joy.
The game signals what kind of challenge, constraint or randomness is coming, so surprises feel designed rather than unfair.
